output.title: Designing against eval drift means setting a stop rule
output.body:
If you are automating a recurring workflow, eval drift is the practical question of when a system stops matching the work it was built to handle. In a small business, that often shows up in customer replies, invoices, or lead handling. The model may look fine on the sample you used to build it, then real messages, edge cases, or a process change pull it off course.

The useful decision is to set the workflow, the measurable outcome, and the stop rule before you automate. For example, if an assistant is classifying inbox messages, decide what “correct enough” means and what level of manual review tells you the system needs a reset. Any threshold is a control, not a promise. If you do not agree it in advance, you are guessing with a nicer interface.

For owner-operators, the boundary is simple: human approval stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions. Eval drift design should help you notice when confidence drops or patterns change, but that is a pilot design choice, not a claim that the system will watch itself forever.

A practical next step is to write one sentence for the workflow: “If X changes, we pause automation and review Y.” Then ask two questions: how will I know this system is slipping, and what decision must stay with me? That turns eval drift from an abstract AI worry into a control you can actually use.
